title: Angophora Song
description: Oil for me always means COLOUR!!! This particular medium - oil paint - is better big and bright for me to work in. I love using a loose, colourful and expressive style with strong contrasts in colour and patterns and the process differs in every way to my drawing work. In some ways I need this as a way of allowing the other side of my personality free. This particular painting was a joy even though I was quite ill whilst doing it - done mostly through a time of lots of bushfire smoke and pollution.\n\nI love painting trees!!! When the wind blows, they seem to dance and move to a music our ears just can't quite hear.

title: Big Swell
description:
102cmx102cm deep canvas.

Starting with fast flow acrylic paint and pouring medium on canvas, I tilted the canvas, allowing gravity to give the paint the shape of waves. I included some metallic gold to represent stirred up sand and was very happy with the way it contrasted with the blues of the water. It still needed something to give a sense of scale to the sea so I included a surfer swimming out to catch the monster wave that seemed to be forming. I called the painting Big Swell in reference to the wave that hadn't yet broken and only later when it was hung realised the other funnier connotations with the surfer's bottom so obvious!

Sold in 2022 to a private collection

title: Mount Fuji and Cherry Blossoms
description: This was a very large commissioned drawing, at the time the largest I'd ever worked on with pen and ink on paper. I used a few different pinks for the flowers and for the grey and black areas, 0.1 finetip black pens. I lost count of how many pens I used... and the drawing had it's own ideas of what it wanted to be, it was a real challenge trying to wrestle it from the brink of chaos. Each flower wanted to be different! I loved the finished work, not just because of how she looked but because she was sooo difficult to do.\n\n12 smaller limited edition Glicee prints on archive quality paper are available of this work. Prices available on request.

title: Claiming Home
description: Oh the pure joy of Rainbow Lorikeets! Such gorgeous rich colours shimmering against the more muted Australian bush tones. Yet that red is in the earth, the green in the sunlight through leaves and the tones of purple and blue in the sky. They are such noisy vibrant personalities that they remind me very much of humans. I also associate with them, the intense emotions I felt when I first arrived in Australia and the feeling of finding Home. I suppose it is why I keep painting them when I am exploring the theme of home for myself.

title: Cockatoo Couple
description:
These two love-birds were seated overlooking my balconey and were a fantastic reference with the interesting colours reflected off their feathers. I also loved how the underlying yellow in their feathers was affected by the sunlight on them, diffusing through and creating an interesting warmth to what is normally a very cold white.

Cockatoos are fascinating, so smart and social but also so destructive at times. A tiny bit like humans.

The Original watercolour (still available) has slightly more detail and a darker background below the branch, please contact me if you wish to see it. Limited edition prints are the same as the shown image, 24/25 prints still available.

title: Fire Horse
description:
In this drawing I wanted to capture a raw, untamed moment of intensity. The horses are locked in combat, their bodies coiled with energy and emotion. Rather than the familiar image of calm, docile farm animals, these horses are fierce and unrestrained, with bared teeth and wild eyes revealing a side of their nature that is powerful, unpredictable, and deeply primal.

The composition is driven by movement and tension. Muscles strain, heads arch, and forms collide, conveying both conflict and vitality. The energy is immediate and visceral, drawing the viewer into the clash. One horse is seeking dominance over the other, but the disadvantaged horse is not ready to submit.

I was initially inspired by a wonderful photo by Susie Bell of wild Salt River horses. I’ve replaced the original cool natural bush tones with a fiery sunset backdrop, an environment that feels less like a physical place and more like an embodiment of the horses’ spirit. Starting with a watercolour wash as a sort of base to work over, I drew over it all with a range of fine tip colour pens. Reds, oranges, and yellows dominate the scene, radiating heat and intensity. I was going to add more red to the actual horses but I really liked the intensity of the white paper against the red background and instead worked it slowly up with many light layers of lines, using both cross hatching and form lines. The drawing process worked its own magic, and I ended up with an image I had not planned but definitely preferred. Against the background, the two fighting horses’ white dappled coats make them appear almost incandescent, as if their inner ferocity is manifesting outward. Their whiteness is not soft, but heat at its most extreme, a white-hot flame that suggests both power and purity of instinct.  There is also a deeper cultural and symbolic layer within the work. Drawing from an Australian perspective, to me the Salt River horses echo the spirit of the Brumbies, wild, independent, and fiercely self-determined. This connection reinforces the theme of freedom and resistance, of creatures that cannot be easily tamed.

Created in recognition of the Year of the Fire Horse, the drawing becomes more than a study of motion and form—it is a tribute to a particular kind of energy: bold, passionate, and unstoppable.

title: Fishing in the Shallows
description: Fishing in the Shallows was created using a mix of acrylic flow, traditional acrylic techniques, highlighted with touches of iridescent and gold paint. I tried to capture the Great Egret's intense gaze and its characteristic knife-like beak as it attempts to eat the unexpectedly large meal. The conflicting narratives underlying the scene are palpable: on one hand, the possibility of the fish being too large and escaping, and on the other, the Egret manages to swallow its prey. This tension invites viewers to decide what they wish the outcome to be.

title: Halfling
description:
This oil painting invites the viewer into a quiet moment where fantasy and the everyday gently intertwine. At its heart, a Halfling (or Hobbit) sits just outside her hidden burrow, absorbed in the simple wonder of a pale moth flitting above her hands, in the glow of her lantern. I intended a scene that was tranquil and grounded, yet quietly enchanted, a world where magic exists not as spectacle, but as something familiar.

Inspired by LoTR and tabletop role-playing worlds, the piece leans away from grand, heroic imagery and instead celebrates a more humble kind of magic. The palette plays a central role in establishing this mood. Rich greens and Burnt Sienna dominate the background, evoking the textures of leaves and tree bark. The lighting suggests early evening. Teal twilight colours in the distance and warm creamy light in the foreground from the lantern, evoking a gentle, diffused glow that enhances the sense of quiet magic.

The background is kept loose and impressionistic, allowing the environment to feel alive and atmospheric. In contrast, the Halfling is painted with greater detail, drawing the viewer’s eye in towards her hands and face and anchoring the composition emotionally. Although the moth is imaginary, it is based on a hawk moth. It becomes both a focal point and a small, luminous bridge between the natural and the magical. Its presence feels playful and personal, hinting at a deeper story just beyond the frame. It is also a nod to the model Nicole’s love of insects and in particular moths. Her online information posts on insects are wonderful.

My source material for this painting were reference photographs provided by the painter and illustrator Howard Lyon (of Nicole), for the character and lighting. I also used some personal photos of the forest walks in the park below my home for the background and colours.

title: Immersed Solo Exhibition
description: Immersed is a series of small paintings that explore the experience of being immersed, in water, a feeling or an environment. This series of paintings were mostly created with many layers of fast flow acrylic and ink drawing. All the works contain some elements of stories, dreams or myths.\n\nFast flowing acrylic is a fairly new medium. I first pour on the initial chaotic layer and then define the emerging shapes with brushwork. The depth is created through the addition of clear layers of acrylic pouring medium. I let the initial layer tell me what story it wants to be and the image gradually evolves.

title: Jerry
description: Jerry is one of my favourite cats even though I have never met him, thanks to daily updates by his human on his shenanigans. My favourite part to paint was his eyes although I enjoyed doing the entire painting. The hardest part was keeping the paint off his whiskers which is the nature of watercolour.\n\nI used my finest, tiniest brush to do the details with a slightly larger fuller brush for washes. The paint is a mix of high quality watercolour paint, mostly Schmincke colours and the paper is Art Spectrum, 300gsm rough Watercolour paper A4 size.

title: Jewelled Dragon
description:
With this version of Spike the Waterdragon, I wanted to emphasise the jewel like quality of his scales so instead of ink, I went with watercolour.

Not overdoing the background was a big challenge and I learnt a great deal whilst working on him as he is by far the largest watercolour painting I'd attempted at this point. Each scale was gone over a few times with different colours and I was very happy with the layered effect by the time I'd finished. It was hard to convince myself to stop painting.

Limited edition prints of "Jewelled Dragon" are available.

title: King I "Legolas"
description:
Winner of the Ku-ring-gai Council Award at the KAS Award Art Exhibition 2019.

A portrait of the local Kookaburra who loves to visit our backyard when we are having a BBQ. With only one leg he waits patiently for morsels of meat before flying off to the next yard. Nicknamed King Legolas (Legless), he is very gentle for a Kookaburra. I did three versions of him, all of which are in private collections.

An original drawing can be commissioned.

title: Meremaid
description: “Mermaid” started as an acrylic pour painting. I wanted to capture the movement of waves with the flow of the paint and then added some rocks using the same technique. I found the image too boring and decided that it was calling for something more.\n\nI added the Mermaid, who then needed more substantial rocks which I brush painted instead of pouring. The Mermaid has interference gold pigment mixed with the acrylic used on her tail so at different angles and light her scales glimmer with a metallic sheen.

title: Mono Vale Beach
description: This was a challenging painting using a combination of fast flow and brush techniques to represent a familiar landscape. I worked from several different photographs and used many layers of paint to create the feeling of the beach at Monavale without being too specific to any particular photo. I also spent several days at the location just getting a sense of the place and doing a few preliminary sketches on site before returning to start the painting in the studio.\n\nSold in 2020 to a private collection

I also spent several days at the location just getting a sense of the place and doing a few preliminary sketches on site before returning to start the painting in the studio.

Sold in 2020 to a private collection
dimensions: Fast flow acrylic paint on large 152cmx122cm canvas

title: Rainbows in The Umbrella Tree
description:
I was inspired by Annabel Armstrong's photographs of Rainbow Lorikeets that were posted on a free to use for artists site. The finished work is a combination of Annabel's references and my own and was an interesting challenge to balance the watercolour and ink drawing techniques together.

I love the pun of them enjoying the nectar of the Umbrella tree and have included a backdrop of the misty/rainy landscape that I often see looking out over the Lane Cove National Park. There are also two little honey bees foraging for nectar in the wet flowers.

The original and some limited edition prints are available.

title: Rainbow Tea Time
description:
This painting, part of a continuing Teatime Still Life series, captures a fleeting yet deeply personal moment, where light, colour, and ritual come together in quiet harmony. Set on a kitchen counter, the scene centres around the preparation of peppermint tea, with my favourite teapot rendered in luminous iridescent blues and purples. Around it sits a collection of rainbow-hued glasses, each one tied to a member of my family, an everyday arrangement that for me is both intimate and symbolic.

What I feel elevated the whole still life was in fact the morning light. Streaming through the glassware, it refracted into a spectrum of colour that danced across the surface and turned a simple every day setting into a celebration of vibrancy and life. I chose to capture the scene midway through the act of making tea as it was too beautiful to not paint. I think this preserved the authenticity of the moment, although I had to remake the tea. It got cold as I was taking reference photo’s.

The painting carries a deeper meaning as well, serving as a tribute to rainbows, neurodiversity, and the full spectrum of human expression. The varied colours of the glasses become more than aesthetic as they suggest individuality within unity, difference held together in a shared, welcoming space.

I also love the ritual of tea making, the quiet contemplative feeling of filling a kettle with boiling water, the rising steam, the smell of tea-leaves and the warmth that comes with sharing it with others.

A rainbow lorikeet appears at the window, peering inside. Bathed in the brilliance of the outdoor light, it contrasts with the softer, more sheltered interior. Its presence suggests curiosity and connection, a bridge between the outside world and the sanctuary within. The kitchen becomes a place of refuge, warmth, and colour, quietly inviting both people and creatures to share in its calm.

Altogether, the painting is a celebration of light, ritual, and belonging, where the ordinary becomes radiant, and the preparation of tea transforms into an expression of comfort, inclusivity, and home.

title: Resting Mermaid
description:
This was a commissioned after a client saw my Mermaid painting at the Easter Show and discovered it had already been bought.

I created this version in a very similar way, with a pour of high flow acrylic paint and pouring medium for the water. I then painted into it to increase the realism.

The client offered to pose for the meremaid and I painted her into foreground once the water had dried, along with the rocks and shallow water. I used irridescent paint for her scales and hair, along with gold acrylic, which gave a pleasing shimmer in changing light.

title: Sir Walter the Brush Turkey
description:
Living on the edge of a National Park means that I get many interesting characters visiting on a daily basis.“ Sir Walter the Brush Turkey” is a portrait of one of the turkeys that pass through my backyard every day. I found him fascinating because as a young turkey he was a nightmare, full of bluster and aggression, he’d chase everyone and was just an overall menace. He then had an encounter with humans as he disappeared for several months and then re-appeared. He’d been given a bright yellow tag on his wing with the number 75, a metal ring on his leg and a crusty wound on the top of his head. Still sporting the same expression on his face, he seemed however to have lost all his cocky bluster and the female turkeys chased him mercilessly instead. Sir Walter had slid all the way to the bottom of the pecking order.

I take many photo’s of the turkeys as their antics are a constant source of amusement and it was from these that I worked from. My favourite one of Sir Walter is the main source for the painting and was taken when he’d regained some of his dominance. His brightly coloured wattle and head show how he was in full courtly mode. I have left off the human tags as I feel it distracts from him, and placed him in a tree as opposed to the balcony railing where he sometimes spends a whole day. The foliage background in the painting is inspired by the view of the Lane-Cove National Park from my balcony and there is even a possum hidden in the undergrowth.

The work is done in watercolour and ink pen on 300gsm watercolour paper. The original is presently exhibited at the Sydney Royal Easter Show.

Limited edition prints in archival ink on watercolour paper are available upon request.

title: Snake in Studio
description:
Second Place  in  CLASS 9 - Drawing  at the  2025 Sydney Royal Arts & Crafts competition

This is a pen drawing of an Australian Diamond Python that regularly sneaks into my studio and suns herself on my window sill, knocking almost everything off in the process. Only the vase - because it is super heavy and the African statue, which is attached with a big dollop of blue tack, were safe from her.

She’s called Domino because of the striking dotty patterns on a glossy dark background that mark her very beautiful skin. In places the markings join to look a little like a variation on the infinity symbol or strange writing, which appealed to me and made me think of the European and Nordic mythologies of Ouroboros.

Snake scales are insane, not only did I have to contend with the complexity of the patterns of her skin but the shape of the scales and the way they change with the angles of her cylindrical shape as her curves change direction and the different sources of light on top of that. Amazing fun and such a challenge that I just didn’t feel I captured as well as I’d like. I definitely would like to do another drawing of her when I have time for another personal project.

Another reason I worked on this drawing this year was because it’s the Year of the Snake so I figured it would be a nice connection to Asia as I seemed to be including something from many of the continents that I feel an affinity to for different reasons and it just felt right.

There is a connection to South America in the Jacaranda tree, which I also had in my backyard in Zimbabwe growing up. Although I omitted the leaves to accentuate the rough branches and trunk which contrast with the lovely smooth eucalyptus tree branches. The Eucalypt leaves I did keep as they tend to be sparse anyway. I wanted the entwined branches to reflect the sinuous flow of Dominos body. I did take some liberty with the view outside the window which includes the trees in my backyard and the Lane-Cove National park bushland that we live on the edge of.

The wooden statue came with the house when we moved in and is one of my favourite items in my studio as it is obviously from Africa. It was such a wonderful thing to find as it is from the continent I was born and grew up on. It does have the look of more West African relics than the statues I am familiar with, from Zimbabwe. From the little research I was able to do on it - it is likely to be a little fertility relic.

The vase is North American (I think but I'm not sure), as is one of the paint brushes. The representation was a bit sparse on that side of things but I didn’t want to add anything unnecessary. I was very amused to discover in drawing the shiny part of the vase that the shapes I could see actually included my reflection taking a photo of the snake so I accentuated that a little and then I discovered another reflection of myself when I drew Domino’s eye, although it is extremely hard to see unless you get up very close to the image.

Initially I found this such a hard drawing to work on. I find the beauty of Domino both mesmerising and disturbing in equal measure. I can’t paint in the studio when she is in there despite knowing she is very unlikely to bite me, She represents to me the true unpredictable and inscrutable nature of the Universe, that we humans are so often sheltered from in our little pockets of urban civility. As I started the drawing the meditative nature of working with pen slowly changed that feeling. I started to see connections I hadn’t noticed and by the end was actually sad that it was complete. It was a very enjoyable drawing to work on.

title: Spike
description: Spike is a Waterdragon that lives in my backyard. I love his regal attitude. This particular pose was taken from a photo my brother Eric Smith took of him whilst bribing him with grapes. He tolerates humans if they feed him but otherwise will run and hide if startled.\n\nHis scales were fascinating to draw. I did not realise how many different shapes they formed until I drew him.

title: Starry Feathers
description:
This painting/drawing was inspired by Matt Laughton’s photo of a female Red Tailed Black Cockatoo. I’ve been wanting to paint one for a while now and had a lot of fun exploring the reflective blues and purple tones on the black feathers. I included a little red-back spider in the corner of the painting. Just a little nod to the colouring of both with the vivid red against the deep black.

They are one of my favourite birds and it is so rare to see them as they are an endangered species. This one has such an interesting expression and a face full of character. The feathers fluffed up around her head so much her face is almost all mohawk and with the way the pale speckles on the feathers spiral around, it does look a little like a galaxy of stars on her face.

The painting was scanned and then I added more ink drawing in the background on the original and so the limited edition versions will be slightly different. The image showed on my website is the limited edition version

title: Summer Seagull
description: The beach exudes a peaceful Summer glow due to the iridescent gold I used in the paint for the sand. It felt too desolate without anyone on it so I chose a seagull to aleviate the lonely feel of it. Despite the seagull's solitude, I feel that there is a serene and contented aura around the bird, as if it's engaged in a silent conversation with it's surroundings.

title: TeaTime
description:
This is a still life that I did as a homage to peppermint tea mornings with a dollop of honey. I loved the morning sunlight on my kitchen counter with the teapot and teacup and reflections on the hexagon tiles.

I did run out of time with this one and wished I had explored the leaves and texture of the teapot a little more but also was fairly happy with the painting as there is a wiggly little part of my brain that tells me that if I had pushed it further I would have overworked it which would have been devastating. The honey was supplied by my Dad who is a beekeeper, the plant was a gift from my friend Henriette. The bees were the only imaginary addition.

I do not have a high resolution version of this painting as I did not have time to get it scanned. Only the original is for sale at this point, in the Sydney Royal Easter Show 2025 exhibition.

This resulted in lovely lush thick fur with tiny variations in colour that I really enjoyed.\n\nHe was painted using a very fine brush for the fur. description: I chose to paint this seagull because it struck me as somewhat cautious, and I found its expression intriguing. So, I made this watercolor sketch to try to capture its attitude. I then added some iridescent watercolor to the background to represent the shimmering world where seagulls live.

title: Water Dragons and Blue Banded Bee
imgTitleAttr: Water Dragons and Blue Banded Bee
description: 2nd place  in  CLASS 3 - Watercolour Painting   at the  2024 Sydney Royal Arts & Crafts competition\n\nThis was a surprisingly fast painting, it took less than a week, despite the detail and size. I was experimenting with a looser style and had to limit myself. I love the expression on the Dragon's face in the foreground - debating whether the bee is edible or a bad idea! A wiser - perhaps more experienced Water Dragon looks on from the background, watching to see what will happen. I added the bee halfway through the painting and loved how suddenly there was a story, just because of how the Dragon needed a reason to be looking up with such curiosity. Sometimes the painting is kind enough to show you what it wants as you are working on it.

description: There is only a small amount of the original pour left in details in the water. This painting ended up being more traditional in approach but that is what it wanted to be. I love the contrast between the wild waves and the calm pelican coming in to land.

title: Woodland Dream
description:
This acrylic painting on canvas started as a simple study of a girl with a beautiful dress and acquired an intriguing life of its own. As I painted her, I realised I really wanted to have her interact with something and the Australian Eastern Water Dragon was the perfect size and attitude to converse with her. I loved the light on her and the contrasting dark of the woodland around her and instead of a super tight, realistic painting that I first intended I ended up keeping most of the initial looseness of the brushstrokes that I marked the scene out with. This has ended up being one of my fantasy works, in keeping with the mermaids and dragons (mythological) that I enjoy doing. To me she seems like a fairy or something otherworldly that has taken on a human appearance, perhaps because she seems to glow.

My source material was a photo by Howard Lyon (model Tessa Halterman) and the dragon was from my personal collection of photos of Prince Stripe in my backyard.

The original painting has been sold but limited edition prints will be available soon

title: Splendid Fairy Wren and Bug
description: This little Splendid Fairy Wren was created from a combination of sources and a large amount of imagination. The bug is loosely based on a flying termite but could be anything really. I thought it just needed to look tasty to a little wren looking for dinner. It started as a small study and then expanded to the whole page as I enjoyed it so much. I kept the colours simple with only a little accent blue on the wrens eye, with warm beak colours and some soft browns on the feathers.\n\nThe original was sold but limited edition prints are available.
descriptionHtml:
This little Splendid Fairy Wren was created from a combination of sources and a large amount of imagination. The bug is loosely based on a flying termite but could be anything really. I thought it just needed to look tasty to a little wren looking for dinner. It started as a small study and then expanded to the whole page as I enjoyed it so much. I kept the colours simple with only a little accent blue on the wrens eye, with warm beak colours and some soft browns on the feathers.

The original was sold but limited edition prints are available.
dimensions: Watercolour and ink drawing on A3 Watercolour paper
